adults.title: From This Day: Realigning Our Lives with Our Covenants
adults.big_idea: When we consider our ways and adjust our lives to make and keep covenants, we are yoked with Jesus Christ and the Lord magnifies our efforts.
adults.objective: Learners will explain what the account of Haggai teaches about priorities and covenants, and will choose one specific adjustment that puts their covenants with God first.
prepare: Read Elder Schmeil's talk, especially the paragraphs on the sacrament and on Haggai.
Bring a paper bag with a few holes cut in the bottom and a handful of coins or buttons.
Bring a slip of paper and a pen for each person.
Write on the board: Doing much. Accomplishing much?

segments.name: A bag with holes
steps: Begin with prayer. If you wish, sing or read the words of I Need Thee Every Hour.
Without explaining, drop the coins into the bag and let them fall through onto the table. Point to the words on the board.
Give each person a slip of paper. Invite one minute of silent writing in answer to the first question below. Tell them no one will see it.
Invite one or two people to share the second question aloud, in general terms.
questions: Where in your life right now are you working hard and still feeling that little is staying in the bag?
What does that kind of tiredness feel like?

segments.name: What happened in Haggai's day
steps: Explain that Elder Schmeil took the title of his talk from the prophet Haggai. The Lord had commanded the Israelites to rebuild the temple, but they did not make it a priority.
Form groups of three or four. Ask each group to read Haggai 1:5–7, 9 and list what was going wrong for the people and the reason the Lord gave.
Read aloud Elder Schmeil's explanation: “Although they were doing much, they were not accomplishing much because God’s holy house was not a priority in their lives.”
Ask the groups to read Haggai 2:19 and find what changed, and when. Point out that, as Elder Schmeil taught, the blessing was promised as soon as they started to rebuild.
Bring the class together for the questions below. Let several people answer before you add anything.
questions: The people were not idle. What is the difference between being busy and being aligned with God's will?
Why do you think the Lord said “From this day will I bless you” at the start of the rebuilding and not at the end?
When have you seen the Lord magnify a small effort to put Him first?

segments.name: Yoked with the Savior
steps: Explain that Elder Schmeil named two divine helps God has given us for mortality: the Savior Jesus Christ and our covenants.
Invite someone to read Matthew 11:28–30 aloud while the class listens for what the Savior invites us to do and what He promises.
Read Elder Schmeil's sentence: “It is through covenants that we become yoked with the Savior Jesus Christ and our burdens become lighter.”
Ask learners to turn to one person nearby and discuss the first question for two minutes, then invite a few to share with everyone.
Share Elder Schmeil's teaching that Heavenly Father is not asking us to physically build a temple; He is asking us to build a strong relationship with Him and His Son through our covenants.
questions: How has keeping a covenant made a burden lighter for you, even when the burden itself did not go away?
What does it look like, on an ordinary weekday, to build a relationship with the Father and the Son through covenants?

segments.name: The weekly covenant
steps: Read together Elder Schmeil's words about the sacrament prayer: we do not need to be perfect to partake; we need to be willing.
Read Elder Renlund's promise, which Elder Schmeil quoted (see aligned quotes). Ask learners to listen for what the sacrament does for someone who comes with a broken heart.
Add Elder Dube's words from this conference (see aligned quotes) as a second witness that we come to Christ as we are.
Discuss the questions. Be gentle; someone in the room may be in that season of hesitation now.
questions: Why might a person hesitate to come to church and partake of the sacrament? What would you want that person to know?
Elder Schmeil said the sacrament has helped him keep his baptismal and temple covenants. How does one covenant help you keep another?

segments.name: Consider your ways
steps: Ask learners to turn their slip of paper over. Give two quiet minutes to write an answer to the question below. Suggest they keep it small and specific: one adjustment, not a new life.
Read the promise Elder Schmeil gave: “He will magnify our efforts as we consider our ways and make the proper adjustments to make and keep covenants with Him.”
As a check for understanding, ask one person to say in a sentence what the people in Haggai's day learned.
Bear your testimony that God keeps His promises. Tell the class that next week you will begin by asking who noticed the Lord magnifying an effort. Next week, do that first.
questions: What is one adjustment that would put your covenants with God ahead of your own house this week?

key_quotes.text: Although they were doing much, they were not accomplishing much because God’s holy house was not a priority in their lives.
It is through covenants that we become yoked with the Savior Jesus Christ and our burdens become lighter.
He will magnify our efforts as we consider our ways and make the proper adjustments to make and keep covenants with Him.
In the sacrament prayer we have a good reminder that we do not need to be perfect to partake of the sacrament.

scriptures.use: Read in groups of three or four; list what was going wrong for the people and the reason the Lord gave.
Read in the same groups; find what the Lord promised and when the promise began.
One person reads aloud; the class listens for the Savior's invitation and His promise, then pairs discuss how covenants yoke us to Him.
Offer as home study: read it this week and mark every blessing King Benjamin names for those who keep the commandments.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dale G. Renlund
aligned_quotes.text: if you follow the Savior’s direction and go and partake of the sacrament, with a broken heart and a contrite spirit, blessings will pour upon you that will keep you firm, that will keep you solid, that will keep you established on that firm foundation that is Jesus Christ.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dube
aligned_quotes.text: We do not need to perfect ourselves to come to Christ. We come to Christ to be perfected.

takeaways: Being busy is not the same as being aligned with God's will.
Covenants yoke us with Jesus Christ, and with Him our burdens become lighter.
The Lord blesses us from the day we begin to put Him first.
act: Make the one adjustment you wrote on your paper, and start it within a day.
Before the sacrament next Sunday, spend five quiet minutes thinking about what the Savior has done for you.
If you have hesitated to come and partake of the sacrament, come anyway, willing and as you are. If you are unsure whether you should partake, talk with your bishop.
Read Mosiah 2:41 and write down one temporal and one spiritual blessing you have received for keeping a commandment.
adapt: At home with two or three adults: skip the groups, read Haggai together aloud, and take turns answering every question.
Large class: keep the Haggai groups to neighbors turning their chairs, and take only two responses per question.
Short on time: do the bag with holes, the Haggai reading, and the closing writing; send Matthew 11:28–30 home as study.

youth.title: Stop Filling a Bag with Holes
youth.big_idea: When we put our covenants with God first, Jesus Christ shares our load and God blesses our efforts.
youth.objective: Youth will explain what the Lord meant by “Consider your ways” in Haggai and will pick one change this week that puts their covenants first.
prepare: Read Elder Schmeil's talk; mark the paragraphs on the sacrament and on Haggai.
Cut the bottoms out of two paper bags. Crumple about twenty sheets of scrap paper into balls.
Bring a blanket or large towel and a tall stack of hymnbooks or other books.
Have paper and pens for anyone without a phone.
Write on the board: Consider your ways.

segments.name: The bag race
steps: Start right after the prayer. Split the class into two teams and give each a bottomless bag and half the paper balls.
One person on each team holds the bag in the air by its top. The team has thirty seconds to fill it. Most balls will fall straight through. Count what stays in.
Laugh with them, then ask the question below. Take two quick answers and move on.
questions: What in real life feels like this: lots of effort and not much to show for it?

segments.name: Find it in Haggai
steps: Tell them the bag is from the scriptures. Elder Schmeil, of the Seventy, built his conference talk on it.
Give the setting in the talk's terms: the Lord had commanded the Israelites to rebuild the temple, but they did not make it a priority.
In groups of three, have them open Haggai 1:5–7, 9 on their phones or in their scriptures and find two things: what was going wrong, and the reason the Lord gave. First group to find both stands up.
Then have everyone read Haggai 2:19 and find what the Lord said once they started rebuilding.
Read Elder Schmeil's summary: “Although they were doing much, they were not accomplishing much because God’s holy house was not a priority in their lives.”
questions: The people were working hard. So what was the real problem?
Why would the Lord promise a blessing on the day they started, before the temple was finished?

segments.name: Carry it together
steps: Lay the blanket on the floor and stack the books in the middle. Ask one volunteer to pick up the whole load alone by gathering the blanket and carry it across the room. Stop them if it is too heavy.
Now have a second person take the other end of the blanket and carry it across together.
Have someone read Matthew 11:28–30 aloud. Explain briefly that a yoke joins two together to pull one load.
Read Elder Schmeil's sentence: “It is through covenants that we become yoked with the Savior Jesus Christ and our burdens become lighter.”
questions: The books did not get lighter. What changed?
When has something hard felt lighter because you prayed, took the sacrament, or kept a promise to God?

segments.name: Answer the text
steps: Read this made-up situation: a friend texts you Saturday night to say they are skipping church tomorrow because they messed up this week and would feel fake taking the sacrament.
Read aloud what Elder Schmeil taught about the sacrament prayer: we do not need to be perfect to partake; we need to be willing to take His name upon us, remember Him, and keep His commandments.
Read Elder Renlund's words that Elder Schmeil quoted (see aligned quotes), and President Oaks's short line from this conference (see aligned quotes).
In pairs, give them three minutes to write a reply to the friend in their own words, kind and honest, using something from what you just read. They can type it in their notes app.
Invite two or three pairs to read their reply. Thank each one. Add that a bishop is glad to help anyone who is unsure about partaking.
questions: Elder Renlund said this hesitation will come to each of us. Why do you think it comes?
What does being willing look like on a week when you have not been at your best?

segments.name: Consider your own ways
steps: Point to the board. Explain that this part is private; no one will be asked to share.
Invite those with phones to look at their own screen time or calendar for the past week. Others can list on paper where their time went.
Ask them to write, just for themselves, an answer to the two questions below.
Read Elder Schmeil's words: “God knows what is best for us and is eager to bless us.” Tell them this is not about guilt. The people in Haggai's day were blessed from the day they turned around.
questions: If someone looked only at where your time went this week, what would they say comes first for you?
What is one small thing you could move so that your promises to God come first?

segments.name: Pick one and start
steps: Ask each person to choose one change from the list of ways to act, or their own, and write it where they will see it, such as a phone lock screen note.
Read the promise from the talk: “He will magnify our efforts as we consider our ways and make the proper adjustments to make and keep covenants with Him.”
As a quick check, ask one volunteer to explain the bag with holes to the class in fifteen seconds.
Share your testimony in a sentence or two. Tell them you will open next week by asking what they changed and what they noticed. Next week, ask.

key_quotes.text: Although they were doing much, they were not accomplishing much because God’s holy house was not a priority in their lives.
It is through covenants that we become yoked with the Savior Jesus Christ and our burdens become lighter.
God knows what is best for us and is eager to bless us.
We need to be willing to take upon us His name, remember Him, and keep His commandments, and in return we have the promise to always have His Spirit with us.

scriptures.use: Groups of three race to find what was going wrong for the people and the reason the Lord gave.
Everyone reads it and finds what the Lord said once the people started to rebuild.
One youth reads aloud after the blanket demonstration; discuss what a yoke does to a load.
Offer as a follow-up for the week: read it and look for the two things the Savior asks of us before weak things become strong.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dale G. Renlund
aligned_quotes.text: the time will come, in each of your lives, when there will be a hesitation to go to church and partake of the sacrament. If it hasn’t happened yet, it will. But know this: if you follow the Savior’s direction and go and partake of the sacrament, with a broken heart and a contrite spirit, blessings will pour upon you that will keep you firm, that will keep you solid, that will keep you established on that firm foundation that is Jesus Christ.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: We are all a work in progress.

takeaways: Busy is not the same as blessed; what I put first matters.
My covenants connect me to Jesus Christ, and He helps carry what I cannot.
I do not have to be perfect to take the sacrament; I need to be willing.
act: Move one thing in your week so a promise to God comes first, such as scriptures before scrolling or prayer before you leave for school.
On Sunday, put your phone away before the sacrament hymn and think of one thing the Savior has done for you.
If a friend has stopped coming, send a kind message this week and offer to sit with them on Sunday.
Read Ether 12:27 and tell the Lord in prayer one weakness you want His help with.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: do the bag race against a timer and write the reply to the friend together.
Large class: run several bag teams at once and have pairs share replies with another pair, not the whole room.
Short on time: keep the bag race, Haggai, and the last two segments; mention Matthew 11:28–30 in one sentence.

children.title: Heavenly Father Loves to Bless Me
children.big_idea: When I put Heavenly Father first and keep my promises to Him, He blesses me.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that Heavenly Father blesses us when we put Him first and will choose one way to put Him first this week.
prepare: A paper bag with holes cut in the bottom, a paper bag with no holes, and a few buttons or small blocks.
Building blocks, or small boxes or books to stack.
A picture of a temple and a picture of the Savior, if you have them.
Paper and crayons for each child.

segments.name: Gather and sing
steps: Invite a child to pray. Sing I Love to See the Temple together.
Sit in a circle. Roll the ball to each child in turn; the child who has it names one good thing Heavenly Father has given them, then rolls it back.
Say: Heavenly Father loves to bless us. Today we will learn about a time He blessed His people.

segments.name: The bag with holes
steps: Hold up the bag with holes. Let children take turns dropping a button into it. Each one falls out. Ask what is wrong with the bag.
Tell them that long ago the Lord told His people their work was like putting things into a bag with holes. They worked and worked, but they had forgotten to put the Lord first.
Hold up the good bag. Let the children drop the buttons in and shake it gently to hear them stay.
Say the truth for today and have the children repeat it: When I put Heavenly Father first, He blesses me.
questions: How would you feel if everything you put in your bag kept falling out?

segments.name: Build the temple
steps: Tell the story simply, as Elder Schmeil told it: The Lord asked His people to build the temple again. They did not do it. Each one hurried to his own house.
Have the children hurry in place and pretend to work on their own houses. Then say: The Lord said, Consider your ways. Children freeze.
Explain that these words mean stop and think about what you are doing.
Say: The people stopped. They were sorry. They chose to obey. Invite the children to come one at a time and add a block to build a temple together. Place the temple picture beside it.
When the first block is placed, tell them the Lord said, “From this day will I bless you.” He blessed them as soon as they started.
questions: When did the Lord say He would bless the people?

segments.name: Stop, think, turn
steps: Place the picture of the Savior on one wall. Have the children stand and walk in place.
Explain the game: when you say Consider your ways, they stop, touch their heads to think, and turn to face the picture of the Savior.
Play four or five rounds, sometimes whispering the words and sometimes saying them slowly.
After the last round, say: Jesus knows each of us. When we turn to Him, He helps us.

segments.name: Draw how I put Heavenly Father first
steps: Explain that we make promises with Heavenly Father. When we are baptized we promise to follow Jesus, and every Sunday the sacrament helps us remember Him.
Ask the children for ways they can put Heavenly Father first. Help with ideas: praying, thinking about Jesus during the sacrament, obeying, being kind.
Give each child paper and crayons. Invite them to draw themselves doing one of these things.
As they draw, go to each child and ask them to tell you about the picture.
questions: What can you think about during the sacrament to remember Jesus?

segments.name: Say it and sing it
steps: Have the children hold up their drawings and say together: When I put Heavenly Father first, He blesses me. Say it once in a whisper and once in a strong voice.
Sing Keep the Commandments.
Read Elder Schmeil's words: “God knows what is best for us and is eager to bless us.” Explain that eager means He really wants to.

segments.name: Choose and close
steps: Ask each child to tell one thing they will do this week to put Heavenly Father first. Their drawing can be the answer.
Tell them in a sentence that you know Heavenly Father keeps His promises.
Ask them to take the drawing home and put it where they will see it. Tell them next week you will ask what they did. Next week, roll the ball again and ask.
Invite a child to pray.

key_quotes.text: God knows what is best for us and is eager to bless us.
Jesus Christ knows us individually, and He will help us if we seek Him
God is our Father in Heaven, and He prepared a plan for us to return to His presence.

scriptures.use: Tell the children this is where the Lord promised to bless His people from the day they began; an older child may read the last sentence of the verse aloud.
Use as the source for the bag with holes and the words Consider your ways; an older child may read verse 7 aloud before the freeze game.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Chigbundu
aligned_quotes.text: I invite you to always remember scriptures, prayers, the sacrament, and covenants.

takeaways: Heavenly Father loves me and is eager to bless me.
When I put Heavenly Father first, He blesses me.
The sacrament helps me remember Jesus.
act: Say a prayer each morning before you play.
During the sacrament on Sunday, sit quietly and think about Jesus.
Put your drawing where you will see it and do what it shows.
music: I Love to See the Temple

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep each part short and skip the questions that need long answers. Let every child drop a button and place a block. Play the stop, think, turn game twice if they are restless, and repeat the one sentence often: When I put Heavenly Father first, He blesses me. Have a helper sit with the youngest while they draw.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: have a child read Haggai 1:7 and the last sentence of Haggai 2:19 aloud, and let an older child lead the stop, think, turn game. Ask a harder question: The people were working hard, so why did the Lord tell them to stop and think? Share Elder Chigbundu's words (see aligned quotes) and ask which of the four things he names they could remember better this week.
